title: Reading Behaviour Without Words
endLine: Behavioural assays measure actions; controls and circuit tests separate their causes.

scenes.tts: A rat cannot say a touch hurts. How do scientists measure pain, fear, or choice without words? They use behavioural assays: standard tests that turn an animal's actions into a measurable stand-in.
scenes.caption: A rat cannot say a touch hurts. How do scientists measure pain, fear, or choice without words? They use behavioural assays: standard tests that turn an animal's actions into a measurable stand-in.
scenes.visual: Dark slate frame carrying one laboratory world: a minimalist side-view test chamber on the left (schematic) and a live readout panel on the right. A rat rests in the chamber as a soft arrow touches its paw and a question mark appears above; when behavioural assays are named, the readout panel illuminates with a moving trial meter (schematic).
scenes.narration: A rat cannot say a touch hurts. How do scientists measure pain, fear, or choice without words? They use behavioural assays: standard tests that turn an animal's actions into a measurable stand-in.

scenes.tts: Start with touch and pain. Researchers press calibrated filaments of increasing stiffness, called von Frey filaments, against a paw. Repeating the test estimates the withdrawal threshold, the force that makes the paw lift. Many labs use the force that lifts it half the time. A fall in that threshold is the rodent sign of allodynia, pain from a normally harmless touch.
scenes.caption: Start with touch and pain. Researchers press calibrated filaments of increasing stiffness, called von Frey filaments, against a paw. scenes.visual: Same chamber: calibrated von Frey filaments of increasing thickness (schematic) rise gently beneath the rat's paw one by one until the paw lifts. On the carried readout panel, a schematic curve plots filament force against paw-lift fraction with a horizontal line marking the threshold many labs use, the force that lifts the paw half the time; the curve then shifts left to lower force as the paw withdraws sooner, labelled allodynia.

scenes.tts: Assays also measure learning through conditioning. In Pavlovian threat conditioning, a harmless conditioned stimulus, like a tone, is paired with a brief footshock. That shock is an unconditioned stimulus because it causes an unlearned reaction. Later, the tone alone triggers conditioned responses: freezing still except for breathing, and rising arterial pressure.

scenes.visual: Same chamber: the filaments retract, a wall speaker sends out gentle sound rings (conditioned stimulus), and a brief floor flash marks the footshock (unconditioned stimulus, schematic). Next, the tone plays alone: the rat holds still with only subtle breathing movement while the carried readout panel transforms into two live schematic traces—a rising freezing bar and an upward arterial-pressure trace.

scenes.tts: Here is the core rule: an assay measures an action, and paired controls separate its causes. Test that idea. Suppose you damage, or lesion, one target below the central amygdala, then condition rats to a tone. If that target drives only arterial pressure, what happens to freezing?
scenes.caption: Here is the core rule: an assay measures an action, and paired controls separate its causes. Test that idea. Suppose you damage, or lesion, one target below the central amygdala, then condition rats to a tone. If that target drives only arterial pressure, what happens to freezing?
scenes.visual: Above the same chamber, a simple schematic diagram of the central amygdala branches into two downward paths feeding the carried readout gauges: arterial pressure and freezing. A small break marks the arterial-pressure branch; a high-contrast question card appears with a pulsing question mark over the freezing gauge.
scenes.narration: Here is the core rule: an assay measures an action, and paired controls separate its causes. Test that idea. Suppose you damage, or lesion, one target below the central amygdala, then condition rats to a tone. If that target drives only arterial pressure, what happens to freezing?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen above the carried chamber and schematic split diagram from the central amygdala. The damaged arterial-pressure branch dims while a slow, steady ring pulses around the freezing gauge for viewers to predict.

scenes.tts: Freezing stays intact while the pressure rise drops. Measuring two responses in the same animal guards against a blunt defect. If freezing survives, the lesion did not block threat learning itself. Still, readouts have strict limits: a paw lift measures a reflex, not a report of pain.

scenes.visual: On the carried readout panel, the arterial-pressure trace drops flat while the freezing bar rises to full height (schematic). The panel then transitions smoothly to a split comparison of the earlier paw-lift meter, separating 'reflex readout' on the left from 'reported pain' on the right.

scenes.tts: Behaviour alone cannot tell which circuit mechanism changed. So scientists pair assays with neural tests. Recording tracks active cells. Stimulation tests whether they are enough, and silencing tests whether they are needed. A lifelong mutant is not an acute change, so when the loss happened matters. Conditions matter too: male and female mice can differ.

Conditions matter too: male and female mice can differ.
scenes.visual: Beside the same chamber, three schematic neural-test icons light up in order on the readout panel: a moving spike trace (recording), a light pulse turning a cell on (stimulation), and a mute gate switching it off (silencing). Below, a lifelong-mutant timeline contrasts with an acute switch flipped in an adult, and two schematic outcome badges contrast male and female mouse conditions.

scenes.tts: Those controls let assays unlock major findings. In 1988, LeDoux, Iwata, Cicchetti and Reis tested threat conditioning in rats. Lateral-hypothalamic lesions impaired the pressure rise while sparing freezing. Lesions in a midbrain region, the caudal periaqueductal gray, disrupted freezing while sparing pressure. Measuring both responses separated two output routes.

scenes.visual: In the same chamber-and-panel world, the carried schematic amygdala diagram splits cleanly into two side-by-side outcome cards tagged 'LeDoux et al., 1988': lateral-hypothalamic lesion flattens the pressure trace while freezing stays high; caudal periaqueductal gray lesion flattens freezing while pressure stays high (schematic).

scenes.tts: In 2009, Sun and colleagues separated itch from pain in mice. They ablated, or killed off, one set of spinal neurons marked by G R P R. Scratching to tested itch stimuli dropped sharply, while measured pain behaviours did not change.
scenes.caption: In 2009, Sun and colleagues separated itch from pain in mice. They ablated, or killed off, one set of spinal neurons marked by GRPR. Scratching to tested itch stimuli dropped sharply, while measured pain behaviours did not change.
scenes.visual: Same chamber, now with a mouse and a small spinal-cord inset showing ablated GRPR-marked neurons (schematic). On the carried readout panel, tagged 'Sun et al., 2009', the schematic scratching bar drops sharply while the schematic pain-behaviour bar remains unchanged.
scenes.narration: In 2009, Sun and colleagues separated itch from pain in mice. They ablated, or killed off, one set of spinal neurons marked by GRPR. Scratching to tested itch stimuli dropped sharply, while measured pain behaviours did not change.

scenes.tts: In 2020, Tan and colleagues offered mice sugar against acesulfame K, equally attractive at first. Preference shifted within twenty-four hours. By forty-eight hours, mice drank almost only sugar, even mice unable to taste sweetness. In this assay, learned preference did not require sweet-taste signalling. Across every test, animal actions become trustworthy evidence only with sharp controls.
scenes.caption: In 2020, Tan and colleagues offered mice sugar against acesulfame K, equally attractive at first. Preference shifted within 24 hours. By 48 hours, mice drank almost only sugar, even mice unable to taste sweetness. In this assay, learned preference did not require sweet-taste signalling. Across every test, animal actions become trustworthy evidence only with sharp controls.
scenes.visual: Same chamber: two drinking spouts slide onto the wall—sugar and acesulfame K (schematic). On the carried readout panel, tagged 'Tan et al., 2020', two schematic bars, equal at first, animate across a time scrubber marked 24 h and 48 h until the sugar bar dominates, even with a crossed-out sweet-taste icon. The three compact discovery badges settle beside the chamber before fading gently.
